intro.title: 1. Introduction
intro.html:
Pluto aims at providing an ultimate user experience in terms of flight experience as well as tinkering. These two experiences are a must for innovation. We believe that tinkerers have great ideas. Some of which can even change the world. We at Drona Aviation strive to help such ideas become reality. Our product Pluto X / Pluto 1.2 is a great prototyping tool for implementing your ideas.

Tinkering is an interesting hobby and the development tool plays a very important role in making it an engrossing experience. A basic development tool will provide a platform where the tinkerer has to begin from scratch every time. However, if a development tool provides an effortless platform for the tinkerers to directly develop their ideas on, without the need of worrying about the rest of the system, it will definitely be more productive.

With this perspective, we do not want our tinkerers to waste their energy in figuring out how to get the drone to fly but to focus only on what they want to do and achieve with the drone. For this purpose, we have done all the work required for the Pluto drone to fly and hence, tinkerers do not need to worry about that. Even without any tinkering, a user can easily fly Pluto X. The entire system has been designed in such an elegant way that the tinkerers can directly start implementing their ideas by coding into the platform provided to them.

platform.title: 3. The Platform
platform.html:
Pluto platform has three essential components: Hardware, Software and Design. All three parts are essential for a seamless flight. The platform allows you to change all three components to suit your needs.

ComponentDescription
HardwareElectronics — the Primus flight controller, sensors, motor drivers, wireless module
SoftwareMagis firmware — provides stable flight, sensor fusion, control loops, and tinkering APIs
DesignFrame, propellers, aerodynamic structure — customizable for new ideas or add-ons

primus.title: 3.1 Primus — The Hardware
primus.html:
Let us understand the hardware that goes into Pluto drones. By hardware, we essentially refer to electronics. The flight controller of Pluto X is called Primus V5 / X2 v1. The flight controller of Pluto 1.2 is called Primus V4. Primus flight controllers come loaded with many features.

Specifications

FeatureDetails
MicrocontrollerSTM32F303CB — 32-bit ARM Cortex-M4 processor, 72 MHz, 256 / 128 Kb flash. Approximately 178 / 50 Kb available for user code; 78 Kb used by firmware.
Wireless ModuleESP12F (ESP Wroom) — generates a WiFi hotspot for connecting your computer and phone. Enables wireless code flashing and flying via Pluto Controller app.
IMU (9-Axis)ICM-20948 — three inbuilt core sensors: Rate Gyro (X, Y, Z), Accelerometer (X, Y, Z, Net_Acc), and Magnetometer (X, Y, Z). Provides orientation, velocity, and acceleration data.
BarometerICP-10111 — measures atmospheric pressure and temperature. Located on the bottom side. Used for altitude estimation.
Voltage & CurrentINA219 — real-time battery voltage and current monitoring.
Internal PowerVin: 2.8V–5.5V, 0A–2A. Logic: 3.3V. 1S battery charger (0.9A–1A).

Motor Drivers

The number of motor drivers depends on the board: Primus V5 has 4 (all unidirectional), while Primus X2 v1 has 6 (the same four plus two extra reversible drivers).

magis.title: 3.2 Magis — The Software
magis.html:
All the hardware is of no use unless coupled with the software, and this combination together makes the Pluto platform whole. Pluto drone runs on Magis, which provides stable flight. Even without any tinkering, a user can easily fly Pluto X.

The Pluto drone runs on the MagisV2-API-Library firmware, which provides a stable foundation for flight and allows tinkerers to program new features. The firmware is structured into logical blocks to separate tasks like data acquisition, estimation, control, and peripherals. Understanding this structure is crucial for programming the Pluto platform.

Core Flight Control Blocks

The primary blocks are responsible for reading sensor data, calculating the drone's state, receiving user input, and controlling the motors.

1. FC-Data (Flight Control Data)

This block is responsible for obtaining and processing the drone's current state.

Sub-BlockData
SensorsAccelerometer (X, Y, Z, Net_Acc), Gyroscope (X, Y, Z), Magnetometer (X, Y, Z), Barometer (Pressure, Temperature)
FiltersProcessing stage where raw data is passed through filtering algorithms (like a Complimentary Filter) to remove noise and prepare it for estimation.
EstimateFiltered and stable state variables: Angle (Roll, Pitch, Yaw), Rate (X, Y, Z), Position (X, Y, Z), Velocity (X, Y, Z)

2. FC-Config (Flight Control Configuration)

This block holds the key parameters and target values used by the control system.

ParameterDescription
User Loop FrequencyDefines the main processing rate of the flight controller (default 3.5ms).
Translational PIDsConfiguration for PIDs controlling forward/backward and side-to-side movement. Includes calculated Desired Position and Desired Velocity.
Rotational PIDsConfiguration for PIDs controlling rotational movement. Includes calculated Desired Angle and Desired Rate.

3. FC-Control (Flight Control)

This block manages the user's commands and high-level flight logic.

Sub-BlockDescription
CommandsARM / DISARM, Takeoff / Land / Flip
Flight StatusCurrent operational state — e.g., Landed, Flying, Armed, Crashed
FC-InterfaceProcesses user input: RC-Data / APP (raw input from controller or app) → RC-Command (processed control command fed into PIDs)
Rx-ConfigReceiver Mode (PPM / ESP) and Channel Config
Flight ModesAngle Mode, Rate Mode, MagHold, AltHold, HeadFree
HeadFree HeadingStores the reference orientation for HeadFree flight mode

4. Motors

This block translates the calculated rotational and translational outputs from the control loop into power signals for the physical motors.

TypeMotorsNotes
RegularM5 – M8Controls the unidirectional motors (standard flight).
Bi-DirectionalM1 – M2Controls the reversible motors. Requires separate initiation via Motor_Init().

Supporting & Peripheral Blocks

These blocks manage essential non-flight functions like power, communication, and expansion.

5. BMS (Battery Management System)

Provides real-time information about the battery's health and usage.

DataDescription
Voltage & CurrentReal-time readings from INA219 sensor
mAh Consumed & RemainingTracks power usage over time
Battery CapacityRated capacity and estimated capacity (calculated)

6. Peripherals & Serial

Access to the drone's low-level hardware communication interfaces.

CategoryInterfaces
PeripheralsADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter), GPIO (General Purpose I/O), PWM (Pulse Width Modulation)
SerialI2C, SPI, UART — communication protocols for external devices

7. Add-Ons

Interfaces for external features and expansion modules.

Add-OnPurpose
OLEDInterface for connecting a display screen
X-RangingInterface for proximity or distance measurement sensors (laser rangefinders)

8. Debugging

Utility functions for monitoring and logging.

ToolPurpose
Monitor_Print / Monitor_PrintlnSend debugging text and values to the Pluto Monitor serial window
TeleplotPlot sensor data in real-time graphs for visual analysis

tinkering.title: Ease of Tinkering
tinkering.html:
No Programming for Normal Flights

Magis continuously runs inside the hardware. Even while tinkering, the core flight software keeps running. Your program runs simultaneously alongside Magis. You never need to re-flash Magis after testing.

Key Point

The drone will fly normally even after your code is flashed. Your code only executes when Developer Mode is ON.

tinkering-loop.title: The Tinkering Loop
tinkering-loop.html:
A separate loop runs just before the Control loop at a default frequency of 3.5ms.

Loop Structure

#include "PlutoPilot.h"

void plutoRxConfig(void) {
  Receiver_Mode(Rx_ESP);    // Onboard ESP
  // Receiver_Mode(Rx_PPM); // PPM based
}

void plutoInit(void) {
  // Hardware init — runs once at power-up
}

void onLoopStart(void) {
  // Runs once when Developer Mode turns ON
}

void plutoLoop(void) {
  // Main loop — runs every 3.5ms
}

void onLoopFinish(void) {
  // Runs once when Developer Mode turns OFF
}
Real-time Warning

Do not use blocking delays or tight while loops inside plutoLoop(). This halts the flight controller. Use the Interval class for time management.

Function Reference

plutoInit()Power-upInitialize extra hardware
onLoopStart()Dev mode ONOne-time setup
plutoLoop()Every 3.5msYour main repeating logic
onLoopFinish()Dev mode OFFCleanup & restore defaults

pluto-ide.title: Pluto IDE – Install & Setup
pluto-ide.html:
Beginner

What is Pluto IDE?

Pluto IDE is a free extension for Visual Studio Code (a popular code editor) made by Drona Aviation. It lets you write your own programs for the Pluto Drone and load them onto the drone — all from one place.

You don’t need any prior experience with drones or embedded programming. Pluto IDE sets up everything for you and gives you simple buttons to build and upload your code.

A few words you’ll see

Firmware = the program that runs on the drone.  Build = turn your code into firmware.  Flash = copy that firmware onto the drone.  Board / Flight Controller = the small computer inside your Pluto.

Works everywhere

Pluto IDE runs on Windows, macOS and Linux.

Before You Start — What You’ll Need

  • A computer running Windows, macOS or Linux.
  • An internet connection (the first-time setup downloads some tools).
  • Your Pluto Drone and a USB cable (for USB flashing).
  • About 10–15 minutes for the one-time setup.

The Whole Journey at a Glance

Here is everything you’ll do, start to finish. Each step has its own page in this guide.

1

Install VS Code

The editor Pluto IDE runs inside.

Download Visual Studio Code
Install Visual Studio Code
2

Install the Pluto IDE extension

From the VS Code marketplace.

Install Pluto IDE from Marketplace
3

Let it set itself up

It downloads the build tools it needs automatically.

Pluto IDE Dashboard
4

Open the Dashboard & sign in

Your home base inside Pluto IDE.

Create New Project wizard
5

Create a project

A guided wizard sets up your code.

Project structure after creation
PlutoPilot.cpp opens automatically
6

Build & flash to your drone

Upload over USB or WiFi.

Step 1 · Install Visual Studio Code

VS Code is a free, open-source code editor. Pick your operating system below.

Windows

  1. Go to https://code.visualstudio.com and click Download for Windows.
  2. Run the downloaded VSCodeSetup.exe and accept the License Agreement.
  3. Keep the default install folder and click Next.
  4. On Select Additional Tasks, tick these boxes:
    • Add “Open with Code” to the right-click menu
    • Add to PATH (important — lets the code command work)
    • Register Code as the editor for supported file types
  5. Click Install, then launch VS Code.
Tip

If you forget to tick Add to PATH, the code terminal command won’t work. You can simply re-run the installer to fix it.

macOS

  1. Go to https://code.visualstudio.com and click Download for macOS.
  2. Unzip the download, then drag Visual Studio Code.app into your Applications folder.
  3. If a security warning appears, open System Settings › Privacy & Security and click Open Anyway.

Linux (Ubuntu / Debian)

Open a terminal and run one of:

sudo snap install --classic code

or, if you downloaded the .deb package:

sudo dpkg -i <downloaded-file>.deb

Step 2 · Install the Pluto IDE Extension

1

Open the Extensions panel

On the left side of VS Code, click the Extensions icon (the four-squares icon), or press Ctrl+Shift+X (Cmd+Shift+X on macOS).

2

Search for Pluto-IDE

Type Pluto-IDE in the search box and pick the one by Drona Aviation.

3

Click Install

Wait for it to finish. The extension activates immediately and a Pluto IDE icon appears in the Activity Bar.

📷
Screenshot — Installing Pluto IDE from the Extensions Marketplace
assets/images/screenshots/install-extension.png
Search “Pluto-IDE” in the Extensions panel and click Install.

Required Companion Extensions (installed for you)

Pluto IDE needs two helper extensions:

  • C/C++ by Microsoft (ms-vscode.cpptools) — understands your code and underlines mistakes.
  • Teleplot by Alex Nesnes (alexnesnes.teleplot) — draws live graphs of data from your drone.

On first use, VS Code prompts you to install them automatically — click Install. Pluto IDE will not work correctly without them.

Two handy tips

• You do not need to restart VS Code after installing — it activates right away.
• If the prompt for the companions doesn’t appear, just search for C/C++ and Teleplot in the Extensions panel and install them manually.

Step 3 · Automatic Toolchain Setup (First Run)

The very first time Pluto IDE activates, it automatically downloads and installs the build tools. You don’t have to do anything — just leave VS Code open and connected to the internet. Progress is shown in the status bar at the bottom of the window. These tools are saved on your computer and reused afterwards, so this only happens once.

What gets installed

  • Cygwin 64-bit (Windows) / native build tools (macOS & Linux)
  • ARM GNU Toolchain — the compiler (arm-none-eabi-gcc)
  • STM32 DFU Driver (Windows only) — needed for USB flashing

Where the tools are stored

SystemFolder
WindowsC:\PlutoIDE\tools\
macOS / Linux~/.pluto-ide/tools/

(Good to know if setup ever fails — deleting this folder and restarting VS Code makes the tools re-download cleanly.)

This download is large

The compiler is a big download (on Windows the full set is over 1 GB), so the first run can take several minutes depending on your internet speed. Let it finish — you only do this once.

Good news for coding

When you create a project, Pluto IDE also sets up code suggestions and error-checking automatically. You don’t need to configure anything. Next stop: the Dashboard. →

p0.title: Project 0: Red LED ON
p0.html:
Beginner

Objectives

  • Understand the basic project structure in Pluto IDE
  • Learn to use the Set_LED() API
  • Learn the build → flash → run workflow

Challenge

Build a project to turn the Red LED ON when Developer Mode is activated.

Explanation

This is your very first project with Pluto. The Primus flight controller has three programmable Status LEDs — Red, Green, and Blue. In normal operation, these LEDs have a default blinking pattern controlled by Magis firmware. To control them yourself, you must first disable the default behaviour using Set_LED(STATUS, OFF) in onLoopStart(), and then set individual LEDs to ON, OFF, or TOGGLE.

Key API

APIDescription
Set_LED(STATUS, OFF)Disables the default LED behaviour
Set_LED(RED, ON)Turns the Red LED ON
Set_LED(STATUS, ON)Restores the default LED behaviour

Solution

#include "PlutoPilot.h"

void plutoRxConfig(void) {
  Receiver_Mode(Rx_ESP);
}

void plutoInit(void) { }

void onLoopStart(void) {
  Set_LED(STATUS, OFF);  // Disable default LED behaviour
  Set_LED(RED, ON);      // Turn Red LED ON
}

void plutoLoop(void) {
  // LED stays ON — no action needed in loop
}

void onLoopFinish(void) {
  Set_LED(RED, OFF);     // Turn Red LED OFF
  Set_LED(STATUS, ON);   // Restore default LEDs
}

Running the Project

  1. Build and flash the project (refer to the Pluto IDE Setup section)
  2. Connect the Pluto Controller App with the drone
  3. Turn Developer Mode ON — the Red LED will turn ON
  4. Turn Developer Mode OFF — the LED will turn OFF and default behaviour resumes
Remember

⇀ All projects are built and flashed the same way
⇀ Your code only runs when Developer Mode is ON
⇀ Always restore defaults in onLoopFinish()

p1.title: Project 1: Takeoff & Land
p1.html:
Beginner

Objectives

  • Learn to use Command_TakeOff() and Command_Land() APIs
  • Understand how onLoopStart() and onLoopFinish() map to Developer Mode ON/OFF

Challenge

Build a program such that the drone will take off when Developer Mode is turned ON and will land when Developer Mode is turned OFF.

Explanation

The Pluto drone has built-in autonomous takeoff and landing routines. The Command_TakeOff(height) API tells the drone to ascend to a specified height in centimeters using the barometer for altitude hold. The Command_Land() API initiates a controlled descent. By placing takeoff in onLoopStart() and landing in onLoopFinish(), you directly tie the drone's flight to the Developer Mode toggle.

Key APIs

APIDescription
Command_TakeOff(150)Auto takeoff to 150 cm altitude
Command_Land()Auto landing with controlled descent

Solution

#include "PlutoPilot.h"

void plutoRxConfig(void) {
  Receiver_Mode(Rx_ESP);
}

void plutoInit(void) { }

void onLoopStart(void) {
  Command_TakeOff(150);  // Auto takeoff to 150 cm
}

void plutoLoop(void) {
  // Flight is maintained by internal control loop
}

void onLoopFinish(void) {
  Command_Land();  // Auto land when Developer Mode is turned OFF
}

Running the Project

  1. Build → Flash → Connect the app
  2. Place drone on flat surface with enough space around it
  3. Turn Developer Mode ON — drone takes off
  4. Turn Developer Mode OFF — drone lands
Safety

If a project involves flying, make sure you have enough space around the drone. Always be ready to disarm from the app if needed.

p2.title: Project 2: RC Pitch → LED
p2.html:
Beginner

Objectives

  • Learn to read RC (Remote Control) stick data using RcData_Get()
  • Understand RC channel values (1000–2000 range)
  • Use conditional logic (if/else) to control LEDs

Challenge

If the Pitch input from the Pluto Controller App is greater than 1500, the Red LED turns ON. If the value is less than 1500, the Red LED turns OFF.

Explanation

The Pluto Controller App sends control stick values to the drone via WiFi. Each stick axis (Roll, Pitch, Yaw, Throttle) sends a value between 1000 (minimum) and 2000 (maximum), with 1500 being the center (neutral) position.

When you move the Pitch stick forward on the app, the RC Pitch value goes above 1500. When you pull it back, it goes below 1500. By reading this value using RcData_Get(RC_PITCH), you can trigger actions based on stick position.

Key API

APIDescription
RcData_Get(RC_PITCH)Returns the current Pitch stick value (1000–2000)
RcData_Get(RC_ROLL)Returns the current Roll stick value
RcData_Get(RC_THROTTLE)Returns the current Throttle stick value
RcData_Get(RC_YAW)Returns the current Yaw stick value

Solution

#include "PlutoPilot.h"

void plutoRxConfig(void) {
  Receiver_Mode(Rx_ESP);
}

void plutoInit(void) { }

void onLoopStart(void) {
  Set_LED(STATUS, OFF);
}

void plutoLoop(void) {
  if (RcData_Get(RC_PITCH) > 1500) {
    Set_LED(RED, ON);   // Pitch stick pushed forward
  } else {
    Set_LED(RED, OFF);  // Pitch stick at center or pulled back
  }
}

void onLoopFinish(void) {
  Set_LED(RED, OFF);
  Set_LED(STATUS, ON);
}
Pro Tip

You do not need to fly or arm the drone for this project. It works even when the drone is on the ground. Just move the Pitch slider in the app and watch the LED respond.

p3.title: Project 3: Dual LED Control
p3.html:
Beginner

Objectives

  • Learn to control multiple LEDs with conditional logic
  • Understand the importance of turning LEDs OFF before switching

Challenge

If RC Pitch is greater than 1500, the Red LED turns ON. If less than 1500, the Green LED turns ON.

Explanation

This project builds on Project 2 by adding a second LED. The key lesson here is state management — when you turn the Red LED ON, the Green LED must be turned OFF, and vice versa. If you forget to turn off the previous LED, both LEDs will remain ON simultaneously, which is not the desired behaviour.

This is a common pattern in embedded programming: always explicitly set the state of all outputs you care about inside each branch of your if/else logic.

Solution

#include "PlutoPilot.h"

void plutoRxConfig(void) {
  Receiver_Mode(Rx_ESP);
}

void plutoInit(void) { }

void onLoopStart(void) {
  Set_LED(STATUS, OFF);
}

void plutoLoop(void) {
  if (RcData_Get(RC_PITCH) > 1500) {
    Set_LED(RED, ON);
    Set_LED(GREEN, OFF);  // Must turn off Green!
  } else {
    Set_LED(GREEN, ON);
    Set_LED(RED, OFF);    // Must turn off Red!
  }
}

void onLoopFinish(void) {
  Set_LED(RED, OFF);
  Set_LED(GREEN, OFF);
  Set_LED(STATUS, ON);
}
Pro Tip

Remember to turn the first LED OFF before turning the other ON. Try intentionally not turning one off and observe what happens — it helps build intuition about LED state control.

p4.title: Project 4: LED Toggle Timer
p4.html:
Beginner

Objectives

  • Learn to use non-blocking timers with the Interval class
  • Understand what TOGGLE means for LED states
  • Learn why delay() must never be used in plutoLoop()

Challenge

The Blue LED will TOGGLE (switch state) after every 2 seconds.

Explanation

Toggle means changing the current state. If the LED is ON, it turns OFF. If it is OFF, it turns ON. Every time the toggle command runs, the LED flips its state.

Since plutoLoop() runs every 3.5ms, you cannot just put Set_LED(BLUE, TOGGLE) directly in the loop — it would toggle 285 times per second, appearing always-on. Instead, you need a timer to ensure the toggle only happens every 2 seconds.

The Interval Class

Pluto provides a non-blocking timer class called Interval. Unlike delay() which freezes the entire processor (and would crash the drone), Interval works by checking elapsed time on each loop iteration without blocking.

APIDescription
Interval myTimer;Declare a timer variable
myTimer.set(2000, true)Set timer to 2000ms (2 sec), repeating
myTimer.check()Returns true when the timer interval has elapsed

Solution

#include "PlutoPilot.h"

Interval toggleTimer;  // Non-blocking timer

void plutoRxConfig(void) {
  Receiver_Mode(Rx_ESP);
}

void plutoInit(void) { }

void onLoopStart(void) {
  Set_LED(STATUS, OFF);
  toggleTimer.set(2000, true);  // 2000ms = 2 seconds, repeating
}

void plutoLoop(void) {
  if (toggleTimer.check()) {
    Set_LED(BLUE, TOGGLE);  // Flip LED state every 2 seconds
  }
}

void onLoopFinish(void) {
  Set_LED(BLUE, OFF);
  Set_LED(STATUS, ON);
}
Pro Tip

Try changing the timer duration to very small values (like 100ms) and observe how fast the LED blinks. This helps build understanding of how the Interval class works.

Never use delay()

Using delay() inside plutoLoop() will freeze the flight controller. The stabilization code, sensor reads, and motor outputs all stop — causing an immediate crash. Always use Interval instead.

p5.title: Project 5: LED Blink
p5.html:
Beginner

Objectives

  • Understand the difference between TOGGLE and explicit ON/OFF blinking
  • Practice using timers for timed actions

Challenge

Blink an LED — turn it ON and then OFF — after every 2 seconds.

Explanation

This project is subtly different from Project 4. In Project 4, each timer tick toggles the state — meaning the LED is ON for 2 seconds, then OFF for 2 seconds (4 second full cycle). In this project, the LED should turn ON briefly and then turn OFF — creating a short "blink" every 2 seconds.

The key insight is: if you turn the LED ON but never explicitly turn it OFF, it stays ON continuously. To create a blink, you need to turn it ON and then immediately (or after a very short duration) turn it OFF within the same timer cycle.

Solution

#include "PlutoPilot.h"

Interval blinkTimer;

void plutoRxConfig(void) {
  Receiver_Mode(Rx_ESP);
}

void plutoInit(void) { }

void onLoopStart(void) {
  Set_LED(STATUS, OFF);
  blinkTimer.set(2000, true);  // Trigger every 2 seconds
}

void plutoLoop(void) {
  if (blinkTimer.check()) {
    Set_LED(RED, ON);   // Brief flash ON
  } else {
    Set_LED(RED, OFF);  // OFF the rest of the time
  }
}

void onLoopFinish(void) {
  Set_LED(RED, OFF);
  Set_LED(STATUS, ON);
}
Pro Tip

If the LED is not switched OFF explicitly, it will remain ON continuously and will not blink. Try changing the time to a very small value (50ms) and observe how it appears as a brief flash.

p6.title: Project 6: Motor PWM Control
p6.html:
Beginner

Objectives

  • Learn to use the Motor_Init() and Motor_Set() APIs for direct motor control
  • Understand the PWM range (1000–2000) for motor speed
  • Learn the importance of shutting motors OFF in onLoopFinish()

Challenge

All motors receive 1200 PWM when Developer Mode is ON, and 1000 PWM (stopped) when Developer Mode is OFF.

Explanation

Motors on Pluto are controlled using PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) signals. The Motor_Init() API initializes a specific motor for direct control, and Motor_Set() sets its PWM value.

PWM ValueMotor State
1000Motor OFF (stopped)
1000–1200Low speed (barely spinning)
1200–1500Medium speed
1500–2000High speed

Normally, the flight controller manages motor speeds automatically through the PID control loop. In this project, you bypass that and directly set motor speeds using the Motor API.

Motor API

APIDescription
Motor_Init(motor)Initializes specified motor for direct control. Must be called in plutoInit().
Motor_Set(motor, pwm)Sets PWM value (1000–2000) for the specified motor.

Available Motors

MotorType
M1, M2Bi-directional (Primus X2 only)
M5, M6, M7, M8Standard flight motors

Solution

#include "PlutoPilot.h"

void plutoRxConfig(void) {
  Receiver_Mode(Rx_ESP);
}

void plutoInit(void) {
  // Initialize all motors for direct control
  Motor_Init(M5);
  Motor_Init(M6);
  Motor_Init(M7);
  Motor_Init(M8);
}

void onLoopStart(void) {
  // Nothing needed here
}

void plutoLoop(void) {
  // Set all motors to 1200 PWM (low speed)
  Motor_Set(M5, 1200);
  Motor_Set(M6, 1200);
  Motor_Set(M7, 1200);
  Motor_Set(M8, 1200);
}

void onLoopFinish(void) {
  // CRITICAL: Stop all motors
  Motor_Set(M5, 1000);
  Motor_Set(M6, 1000);
  Motor_Set(M7, 1000);
  Motor_Set(M8, 1000);
}
Critical Safety Rule

Whenever you control motors using PWM, always shut them OFF by setting 1000 PWM inside onLoopFinish(). This ensures motors don't keep running when Developer Mode is turned OFF or when the app gets disconnected. Failing to do this is dangerous.

p7.title: Project 7: Desired Yaw
p7.html:
Beginner

Objectives

  • Learn to set a desired orientation using setDesiredAngle()
  • Understand the Yaw axis (rotation around the vertical axis)
  • Combine LED indication with flight commands

Challenge

Turn the Green LED and Blue LED ON, and make the drone yaw to 150 degrees.

Explanation

The Yaw angle represents the drone's heading — the direction it is facing when viewed from above. A yaw of 0° means the drone faces North (when magnetometer is calibrated), 90° is East, 180° is South, and 270° is West.

The setDesiredAngle(AG_YAW, value) API tells the flight controller to rotate the drone to the specified heading. The internal PID controller handles the motor adjustments to achieve this angle.

Key API

APIDescription
setDesiredAngle(AG_YAW, 150)Rotate drone to face 150° heading
setDesiredAngle(AG_ROLL, value)Set desired Roll angle
setDesiredAngle(AG_PITCH, value)Set desired Pitch angle

Solution

#include "PlutoPilot.h"

void plutoRxConfig(void) {
  Receiver_Mode(Rx_ESP);
}

void plutoInit(void) { }

void onLoopStart(void) {
  Set_LED(STATUS, OFF);
  Set_LED(GREEN, ON);
  Set_LED(BLUE, ON);
}

void plutoLoop(void) {
  setDesiredAngle(AG_YAW, 150);  // Rotate drone to 150 degrees
  Monitor_Println("Yaw:", Estimate_Get(Angle, AG_YAW));
}

void onLoopFinish(void) {
  Set_LED(GREEN, OFF);
  Set_LED(BLUE, OFF);
  Set_LED(STATUS, ON);
}
Pro Tip

Desired State commands (like Desired Yaw) can be tested only while flying the drone. The drone must be armed and airborne. On the ground, the motors will try to spin but the drone won't rotate properly.

p8.title: Project 8: Roll Angle → LED
p8.html:
Beginner

Objectives

  • Learn to read real-time sensor data using Estimate_Get()
  • Understand Roll angle and how tilting the drone changes it
  • Practice using sensor data to drive visual output

Challenge

If the current Roll angle is between -180° and 0°, the Red LED turns ON. If the Roll angle is between 0° and 180°, the Green LED turns ON.

Explanation

The Roll angle represents how much the drone is tilted sideways. When the drone is level, Roll ≈ 0°. Tilting to the right increases Roll (positive), tilting to the left decreases it (negative). The range is -180° to +180°.

The Estimate_Get(Angle, AG_ROLL) API returns the current Roll angle in deciDegrees (i.e., 10× the actual degrees — so 450 means 45.0°). This gives you higher precision.

Key API

APIReturns
Estimate_Get(Angle, AG_ROLL)Current Roll angle in deciDegrees
Estimate_Get(Angle, AG_PITCH)Current Pitch angle in deciDegrees
Estimate_Get(Angle, AG_YAW)Current Yaw angle in degrees

Solution

#include "PlutoPilot.h"

void plutoRxConfig(void) {
  Receiver_Mode(Rx_ESP);
}

void plutoInit(void) { }

void onLoopStart(void) {
  Set_LED(STATUS, OFF);
}

void plutoLoop(void) {
  int16_t roll = Estimate_Get(Angle, AG_ROLL);

  if (roll < 0) {
    // Roll is negative (-180 to 0) — tilted left
    Set_LED(RED, ON);
    Set_LED(GREEN, OFF);
  } else {
    // Roll is positive (0 to 180) — tilted right
    Set_LED(GREEN, ON);
    Set_LED(RED, OFF);
  }

  Monitor_Println("Roll:", roll);
}

void onLoopFinish(void) {
  Set_LED(RED, OFF);
  Set_LED(GREEN, OFF);
  Set_LED(STATUS, ON);
}
Pro Tip

A single challenge can have multiple solutions. You could check Roll > 0 in one condition and use else for the other, or you could use two separate if blocks with explicit ranges. Try both and identify the most optimum approach.

No flying needed

This project works by simply holding and tilting the drone in your hand. No need to arm or fly.

p9.title: Project 9: Color Wheel
p9.html:
Intermediate

Objectives

  • Learn how the Magnetometer measures the Yaw angle
  • Understand primary and secondary color mixing using RGB LEDs
  • Practice using multiple conditional ranges

Challenge

As the drone yaws (rotates) through 360°, it should generate different primary and secondary colors using the onboard LEDs.

The Idea

A color wheel shows how primary colors (Red, Green, Blue) combine to form secondary colors (Yellow, Cyan, Magenta). Since the Primus flight controller has Red, Green, and Blue LEDs, by turning ON different combinations at specific yaw angle ranges, you can create a live color wheel.

Color Mapping

Yaw RangeLEDs ONColor Produced
0° – 60°RedRed
60° – 120°Red + GreenYellow
120° – 180°GreenGreen
180° – 240°Green + BlueCyan
240° – 300°BlueBlue
300° – 360°Blue + RedMagenta

Approach

Read the current Yaw angle using Estimate_Get(Angle, AG_YAW), then use a series of if/else conditions to turn on the appropriate LED combination for each 60° range.

Solution

#include "PlutoPilot.h"

void plutoRxConfig(void) {
  Receiver_Mode(Rx_ESP);
}

void plutoInit(void) { }

void onLoopStart(void) {
  Set_LED(STATUS, OFF);
}

void plutoLoop(void) {
  int16_t yaw = Estimate_Get(Angle, AG_YAW);

  // Turn all LEDs off first
  Set_LED(RED, OFF);
  Set_LED(GREEN, OFF);
  Set_LED(BLUE, OFF);

  // Map yaw angle to colors (60 degree segments)
  if (yaw >= 0 && yaw < 60) {
    Set_LED(RED, ON);                   // Red
  } else if (yaw >= 60 && yaw < 120) {
    Set_LED(RED, ON);
    Set_LED(GREEN, ON);                  // Yellow (Red+Green)
  } else if (yaw >= 120 && yaw < 180) {
    Set_LED(GREEN, ON);                  // Green
  } else if (yaw >= 180 && yaw < 240) {
    Set_LED(GREEN, ON);
    Set_LED(BLUE, ON);                   // Cyan (Green+Blue)
  } else if (yaw >= 240 && yaw < 300) {
    Set_LED(BLUE, ON);                   // Blue
  } else {
    Set_LED(BLUE, ON);
    Set_LED(RED, ON);                    // Magenta (Blue+Red)
  }
}

void onLoopFinish(void) {
  Set_LED(RED, OFF);
  Set_LED(GREEN, OFF);
  Set_LED(BLUE, OFF);
  Set_LED(STATUS, ON);
}
Insights

⇀ The Magnetometer is the sensor responsible for measuring the Yaw angle
⇀ If yaw values seem unstable or wrong, perform Magnetometer Calibration from the Pluto Controller App
⇀ This project does not require flying or arming — just rotate the drone by hand on a flat surface

p10.title: Project 10: Compass Drone
p10.html:
Intermediate

Objectives

  • Understand how a digital compass works using the Magnetometer
  • Learn to set the desired yaw angle to point in compass directions
  • Use LEDs as direction indicators

Challenge

Use your Pluto drone as a digital compass to point towards North, East, South, and West.

The Idea

Compasses have been used since ancient times for navigation. A traditional compass points towards Earth's magnetic North. The Magnetometer sensor on Primus does the same thing — when properly calibrated, a yaw angle of 0° corresponds to North.

Direction Mapping

Yaw AngleDirectionLED Indicator
0°NorthRed
90°EastGreen
180°SouthBlue
270°WestRed + Green

Approach

By setting the desired yaw angle using setDesiredAngle(AG_YAW, angle), the drone's internal control system will rotate it to face the specified direction. Use different LED colors for each cardinal direction so you can visually confirm which way the drone is pointing.

Solution

#include "PlutoPilot.h"

void plutoRxConfig(void) {
  Receiver_Mode(Rx_ESP);
}

void plutoInit(void) { }

void onLoopStart(void) {
  Set_LED(STATUS, OFF);
}

void plutoLoop(void) {
  int16_t yaw = Estimate_Get(Angle, AG_YAW);

  Set_LED(RED, OFF);
  Set_LED(GREEN, OFF);
  Set_LED(BLUE, OFF);

  // Indicate current cardinal direction with LEDs
  if (yaw >= 315 || yaw < 45) {
    Set_LED(RED, ON);                    // North
    Monitor_Println("North:", yaw);
  } else if (yaw >= 45 && yaw < 135) {
    Set_LED(GREEN, ON);                  // East
    Monitor_Println("East:", yaw);
  } else if (yaw >= 135 && yaw < 225) {
    Set_LED(BLUE, ON);                   // South
    Monitor_Println("South:", yaw);
  } else {
    Set_LED(RED, ON);
    Set_LED(GREEN, ON);                  // West (Yellow)
    Monitor_Println("West:", yaw);
  }
}

void onLoopFinish(void) {
  Set_LED(RED, OFF);
  Set_LED(GREEN, OFF);
  Set_LED(BLUE, OFF);
  Set_LED(STATUS, ON);
}
Fun Activity

⇀ With friends, try guessing directions inside a room with no sunlight
⇀ Use this project to verify the actual compass directions
⇀ The person with the closest guess wins!

p11.title: Project 11: Spirit Level
p11.html:
Intermediate

Objectives

  • Use the drone as a measurement tool (digital spirit level)
  • Learn to define an acceptable error range (dead zone)
  • Combine blinking LEDs with sensor thresholds

Challenge

Build a program to use Pluto as a digital spirit level and detect whether a surface is perfectly horizontal.

The Idea

Traditional spirit levels use a bubble in a tube of liquid to check if a surface is horizontal. With Pluto, you can build a smart, digital version using the drone's accelerometer and gyroscope — which continuously measure the Roll and Pitch angles.

Approach

Read the current Roll angle using Estimate_Get(Angle, AG_ROLL). Define a small acceptable range (e.g., -50 to +50 deciDegrees, which is ±5°) as the "level" zone:

  • If Roll is within the level zone → steady Green LED indicates the surface is balanced
  • If Roll is outside the zone → Red LED blinks to indicate the surface is tilted
  • The faster the blink, the more tilted the surface (use Interval class for blink speed)

Solution

#include "PlutoPilot.h"

Interval blinkTimer;

void plutoRxConfig(void) {
  Receiver_Mode(Rx_ESP);
}

void plutoInit(void) { }

void onLoopStart(void) {
  Set_LED(STATUS, OFF);
  blinkTimer.set(200, true);  // Fast blink for tilt warning
}

void plutoLoop(void) {
  int16_t roll = Estimate_Get(Angle, AG_ROLL);

  // Level zone: within +/- 5 degrees (50 deciDegrees)
  if (roll > -50 && roll < 50) {
    Set_LED(GREEN, ON);   // Surface is level — steady green
    Set_LED(RED, OFF);
  } else {
    Set_LED(GREEN, OFF);  // Surface is tilted — blink red
    if (blinkTimer.check()) {
      Set_LED(RED, TOGGLE);
    }
  }

  Monitor_Println("Roll:", roll);
}

void onLoopFinish(void) {
  Set_LED(RED, OFF);
  Set_LED(GREEN, OFF);
  Set_LED(STATUS, ON);
}
Insights

⇀ Changing the Interval timer duration affects how fast the LED blinks
⇀ You can customize accuracy by modifying the acceptable angle range
⇀ Try adding Pitch detection to make it work in both directions

p12.title: Project 12: Truth or Dare
p12.html:
Intermediate

Objectives

  • Use random number generation in embedded programming
  • Combine timers with desired yaw angle control
  • Build an interactive game using a drone

Challenge

Build a fun game where a spinning drone replaces the traditional spinning bottle to play Truth or Dare.

The Idea

In the classic Truth or Dare game, a bottle is spun to randomly select a participant. In this upgraded version, the Pluto drone itself spins in the air and points toward a participant when it stops. The selected person must then choose between Truth or Dare.

Approach

  • Generate a random yaw angle (0–360°) to create surprise
  • Use setDesiredAngle(AG_YAW, randomAngle) to spin the drone
  • Use a timer so the drone gets enough time to reach an angle before receiving the next random angle
  • Fly the drone in Headfree mode for easier control during the game

Participant Setup

PositionYaw Angle
Player 10° (North)
Player 290° (East)
Player 3180° (South)
Player 4270° (West)

Solution

#include "PlutoPilot.h"

Interval spinTimer;
int16_t targetYaw = 0;

void plutoRxConfig(void) {
  Receiver_Mode(Rx_ESP);
}

void plutoInit(void) { }

void onLoopStart(void) {
  Set_LED(STATUS, OFF);
  spinTimer.set(5000, true);  // Pick new player every 5 seconds
  targetYaw = 0;
}

void plutoLoop(void) {
  if (spinTimer.check()) {
    // Use sensor noise for randomness (0, 90, 180, or 270)
    int16_t raw = Sensor_Get(Gyroscope, X);
    if (raw < 0) raw = -raw;
    int player = raw % 4;
    targetYaw = player * 90;

    Set_LED(RED, TOGGLE);   // Visual feedback: new spin
    Set_LED(BLUE, TOGGLE);
  }

  setDesiredAngle(AG_YAW, targetYaw);
  Monitor_Println("Player at:", targetYaw);
}

void onLoopFinish(void) {
  Set_LED(RED, OFF);
  Set_LED(BLUE, OFF);
  Set_LED(STATUS, ON);
}
Game Rules

⇀ Play with 4 participants standing at 0°, 90°, 180°, and 270° relative to the drone
⇀ When the drone stops spinning, the person it points to must choose Truth or Dare

Activity

Modify the code so the game can be played by 6 participants instead of 4. Think about how yaw angles should be divided equally! (Hint: 360° / 6 = 60° per participant)

p13.title: Project 13: Chuck to Arm
p13.html:
Intermediate

Objectives

  • Understand the concept of free fall
  • Learn how an accelerometer works and what it measures
  • Use sensor thresholds to trigger flight commands

Challenge

Arm Pluto X by tossing it in the air instead of arming it traditionally by keeping it on a flat surface.

Explanation: Free Fall

Einstein's Elevator Thought Experiment (1907) showed that gravity is nothing but an acceleration. When an object is tossed in the air and leaves the hand, the only force acting on it is gravity — it is under free fall. All objects, regardless of size or weight, free fall with the same acceleration:

a = W / m = (m × g) / m = g

Even if a body moves upwards, if there is no force acting on it other than gravity, it is under free fall. Don't let the name "fall" confuse you.

Explanation: Accelerometer

An accelerometer measures Proper Acceleration — the acceleration of a body measured with respect to a freely falling object. It uses capacitive MEMS technology where movable plates shift with acceleration, changing the capacitance C = εA/d.

ConditionAccelerometer Reading
At rest on flat surface≈ 1g upward (≈ 512 raw units)
In free fall (tossed)≈ 0g (approaching zero)
During a crash> 2g (high impact)

Approach

The logic: when the net acceleration value goes below 2 (approaching free fall) and Pluto X is not in a crashed state, arm the drone. Both conditions must be satisfied.

Code

#include "PlutoPilot.h"

void plutoRxConfig(void) { Receiver_Mode(Rx_ESP); }
void plutoInit(void) { }

void onLoopStart(void) {
  Set_LED(STATUS, OFF);
}

void plutoLoop(void) {
  // Detect free fall: net acceleration approaching zero
  // Also ensure drone hasn't crashed
  if (Sensor_Get(Accelerometer, Net_Acc) < 2
      && !FlightStatus_Check(FS_CRASHED)) {
    Command_Arm();       // Arm the drone
    Set_LED(RED,   ON);  // Visual confirmation
    Set_LED(GREEN, ON);
  }
}

void onLoopFinish(void) {
  Set_LED(STATUS, ON);  // Restore default LEDs
}

Running the Project

  1. Build → Flash → Turn Developer Mode ON
  2. Toss Pluto X gently in the air
  3. The LEDs turn on and the drone arms mid-air!
Safety

⇀ Toss the drone gently — do not throw aggressively
⇀ Always perform this in an open, safe area
⇀ The crash check prevents arming during actual crashes

Key Takeaway

An accelerometer cannot distinguish between gravity and any other acceleration — just like a person in Einstein's elevator. By understanding the physics of free fall, you can build clever features using simple sensor thresholds.

p14.title: Project 14: Open Sesame
p14.html:
Intermediate

Objectives

  • Understand how a Barometer measures atmospheric pressure
  • Use environmental changes (air pressure) to trigger drone actions
  • Learn about low-pass filtering for sensor data

Challenge

Make the drone arm and take off when there is a considerable change in atmospheric pressure — for example, when a door is opened or closed swiftly near the drone.

Explanation: Barometer

A barometer measures atmospheric pressure. The MEMS barometer in Pluto works on the principle of mechanical bending of a silicon diaphragm by gas pressure. The bending changes the distance between metallic plates, changing capacitance: C = εA/d

Key Relationship

ChangePressure Effect
Higher altitudeLower atmospheric pressure
Lower altitudeHigher atmospheric pressure
Door opened/closed swiftlyMomentary pressure spike or dip
Blowing air on sensorTemporary pressure change

Barometers are preferred over GPS for altitude measurement due to their higher accuracy (up to 10 cm when combined with temperature compensation).

Approach

Record the initial pressure when Developer Mode turns ON. Continuously compare current pressure to this baseline. When the difference exceeds a threshold (e.g., 8 units), trigger the drone to arm and take off.

A low-pass filter is used to slowly update the baseline pressure, preventing gradual drift from triggering a false detection:

initPressure = (initPressure × 0.9) + (currPressure × 0.1)

Code

#include "PlutoPilot.h"
int initPressure, currPressure;

void plutoRxConfig(void) { Receiver_Mode(Rx_ESP); }
void plutoInit(void) { }

void onLoopStart(void) {
  initPressure = Sensor_Get(Barometer, Pressure);
  Set_LED(STATUS, OFF);
}

void plutoLoop(void) {
  currPressure = Sensor_Get(Barometer, Pressure);

  if (abs(currPressure - initPressure) > 8) {
    Set_LED(RED, ON);
    Command_Arm();
    Monitor_Print("Drone Armed");
    setDesiredPosition(Z, 100);  // Take off to 100 cm
  }

  // Low-pass filter to track baseline drift
  initPressure = (initPressure * 0.9) + (currPressure * 0.1);
  Monitor_Println("Diff:", currPressure - initPressure);
}

void onLoopFinish(void) {
  Set_LED(STATUS, ON);
}

Running the Project

  1. Build → Flash → Get in a closed room
  2. Connect with Pluto Controller app, turn Developer Mode ON
  3. Open or close the door swiftly — the drone detects the pressure change and takes off!
Note

If the pressure difference doesn't exceed 8, Pluto X will not take off. In that case, change the threshold to a smaller value in the code. You can also try blowing directly on the barometer sensor.

Key Takeaway

Environmental conditions can be used for feature development. Different sensors detect different environmental changes — e.g., a fire-fighting drone could use a temperature sensor, a pollution-monitoring drone could use a chemical sensor.

p15.title: Project 15: Gyroscopic Drone
p15.html:
Intermediate

Objectives

  • Understand how the Gyroscope sensor works (Coriolis Effect)
  • Learn the difference between angle and rate of rotation
  • Directly map sensor data to motor output

Challenge

Experience the effect of the Gyroscope sensor by powering the motors using only gyroscope data while holding Pluto in your hand.

Explanation: Gyroscope

MEMS gyroscopes measure angular velocity — the speed of rotation in degrees per second (°/s). They work on the principle of the Coriolis Effect: a tiny resonating mass inside the sensor gets deflected when rotated, and the deflection is converted into an electrical signal.

The gyroscope is the most critical sensor in a drone — it provides stability by detecting how fast the drone is rotating on each axis (Pitch, Roll, Yaw) and feeding this data into the PID controller.

Key Difference

SensorMeasuresExample
AccelerometerTilt angle (static orientation)"The drone is tilted 30° to the right"
GyroscopeRate of rotation (how fast it's spinning)"The drone is rotating at 200°/s to the right"

Approach

Instead of using the normal flight controller, this project reads raw gyroscope values and maps them directly to motor speeds:

  • Positive gyro values → power one set of motors (e.g., M5, M7)
  • Negative gyro values → power the opposite set (e.g., M6, M8)

This creates an intuitive physical feedback: tilt the drone and feel the motors respond.

Solution

#include "PlutoPilot.h"

void plutoRxConfig(void) {
  Receiver_Mode(Rx_ESP);
}

void plutoInit(void) { }

void onLoopStart(void) {
  Set_LED(STATUS, OFF);
}

void plutoLoop(void) {
  int16_t gyroX = Sensor_Get(Gyroscope, X);  // Roll axis rate

  if (gyroX > 10) {
    // Rotating right — power left-side motors
    RcCommand_Set(RC_ROLL, 1500 + (gyroX / 2));
    Set_LED(RED, ON);
    Set_LED(GREEN, OFF);
  } else if (gyroX < -10) {
    // Rotating left — power right-side motors
    RcCommand_Set(RC_ROLL, 1500 + (gyroX / 2));
    Set_LED(GREEN, ON);
    Set_LED(RED, OFF);
  } else {
    // No rotation — neutral
    RcCommand_Set(RC_ROLL, 1500);
    Set_LED(RED, OFF);
    Set_LED(GREEN, OFF);
  }

  Monitor_Println("GyroX:", gyroX);
}

void onLoopFinish(void) {
  RcCommand_Set(RC_ROLL, 1500);  // Reset to neutral
  Set_LED(RED, OFF);
  Set_LED(GREEN, OFF);
  Set_LED(STATUS, ON);
}
Activity

⇀ Try changing the inclination about the roll axis very slowly without making the motors rotate
⇀ This demonstrates that gyroscopes measure rate of rotation, not the angle itself — if you tilt very slowly, the angular velocity is near zero even though the angle changes

p16.title: Project 16: Logic Drone
p16.html:
Intermediate

Objectives

  • Understand Logic Gates (AND, OR) — the foundation of digital electronics
  • Use RC stick inputs as logical inputs
  • Visualize abstract logic operations using physical hardware

Challenge

Demonstrate AND and OR logic gates using the Pluto Controller App sticks as inputs and the drone's motors and LEDs as outputs.

Explanation: Logic Gates

Logic gates are the building blocks of all digital electronics — from smartphones to satellites. They take binary inputs (true/false, HIGH/LOW) and produce a single output based on a rule.

GateRuleExample
ANDOutput is true only if both inputs are trueThrottle UP AND Pitch UP → Motors ON
OROutput is true if either input is trueThrottle UP OR Pitch UP → LED ON

Approach

The Pluto Controller App sticks serve as inputs:

  • Throttle stick > 1500 = Input A is HIGH
  • Pitch stick > 1500 = Input B is HIGH

Apply AND/OR logic to these inputs and show the result using motors and LEDs.

Solution

#include "PlutoPilot.h"

void plutoRxConfig(void) {
  Receiver_Mode(Rx_ESP);
}

void plutoInit(void) { }

void onLoopStart(void) {
  Set_LED(STATUS, OFF);
}

void plutoLoop(void) {
  bool inputA = (RcData_Get(RC_THROTTLE) > 1500);  // Throttle stick
  bool inputB = (RcData_Get(RC_PITCH) > 1500);     // Pitch stick

  // AND Gate: Both HIGH -> Red LED ON
  if (inputA && inputB) {
    Set_LED(RED, ON);
  } else {
    Set_LED(RED, OFF);
  }

  // OR Gate: Either HIGH -> Green LED ON
  if (inputA || inputB) {
    Set_LED(GREEN, ON);
  } else {
    Set_LED(GREEN, OFF);
  }

  Monitor_Println("AND:", (inputA && inputB) ? 1 : 0);
  Monitor_Println("OR:", (inputA || inputB) ? 1 : 0);
}

void onLoopFinish(void) {
  Set_LED(RED, OFF);
  Set_LED(GREEN, OFF);
  Set_LED(STATUS, ON);
}
Insight

This project shows how abstract logic operations directly control physical systems like motors and LEDs. Every electronic device you use — phone, computer, car — uses millions of these logic gates working together.

p17.title: Project 17: One Key Return
p17.html:
Intermediate

Objectives

  • Use the phone's heading (magnetometer) to guide the drone
  • Implement heading error correction between phone and drone
  • Build a simplified "return to pilot" feature without GPS

Challenge

Build a program to call the drone back to the pilot by toggling Developer Mode — without using GPS.

The Idea

Normally, "Return to Home" features require GPS to know the drone's position. In this project, you use a simpler approach: the Pluto Controller App sends the phone's heading (yaw angle from the phone's magnetometer) to the drone. By comparing the drone's heading with the phone's heading, the drone can:

  1. Rotate to face toward the pilot
  2. Move forward to fly back

Approach

  • Read the phone heading using App_getAppHeading()
  • Read the drone heading using Estimate_Get(Angle, AG_YAW)
  • Calculate the error (difference) between the two headings
  • Set the drone's desired yaw to match the phone heading (corrected for initial offset)
  • Optionally add forward pitch to make the drone fly toward the pilot

Solution

#include "PlutoPilot.h"
#include "RC-Interface.h"

int16_t Error = 0;
int16_t PlutoXHeading = 0;

void plutoRxConfig(void) {
  Receiver_Mode(Rx_ESP);
}

void plutoInit(void) { }

void onLoopStart(void) {
  Set_LED(STATUS, OFF);
  // Calculate initial offset between phone and drone heading
  Error = App_getAppHeading() - Estimate_Get(Angle, AG_YAW);
  Monitor_Println("Offset:", Error);
}

void plutoLoop(void) {
  // Correct phone heading by removing offset
  PlutoXHeading = App_getAppHeading() - Error;
  if (PlutoXHeading < 0)   PlutoXHeading += 360;
  if (PlutoXHeading > 360) PlutoXHeading -= 360;

  // Point drone toward pilot
  setDesiredAngle(AG_YAW, PlutoXHeading);

  // Slight forward pitch to fly back
  RcCommand_Set(RC_PITCH, 1550);

  Set_LED(GREEN, ON);
  Monitor_Println("Heading:", PlutoXHeading);
}

void onLoopFinish(void) {
  RcCommand_Set(RC_PITCH, 1500);  // Stop forward motion
  Set_LED(GREEN, OFF);
  Set_LED(STATUS, ON);
}
Setup Required

⇀ In the Pluto Controller app: go to Developer Settings → Turn ON "Send Heading"
⇀ The app will start sending the phone's compass heading to the drone
⇀ Variables needed: Error (int16_t), PlutoXHeading (int16_t), Flag (bool)

Key Takeaway

This project demonstrates that navigation doesn't always require GPS. Relative heading between two magnetometers (phone and drone) provides enough information for basic return-to-pilot functionality.

p18.title: Project 18: Hooter Module
p18.html:
Advanced

Objectives

  • Learn to use GPIO pins for controlling external hardware
  • Interface an external buzzer module with the Primus board
  • Combine timers with GPIO output for periodic beeping

Challenge

Make your Pluto drone produce a beeping sound using an external buzzer (hooter) module connected to the GPIO port.

Add-On: Buzzer Module

Pluto X supports many add-ons through its Unibus and GPIO ports. The Hooter Module is a simple passive buzzer that makes sound when it receives power. It is commonly used for alerts, alarms, or status beeps.

Connection

Connect the buzzer module to the RC port on the Primus V5 / X2 board:

Buzzer PinPrimus Pin
GNDGND
Signal / VCCGPIO_1

How it Works

  1. On start (onLoopStart): Initialize GPIO_1 as OUTPUT, set it LOW, start a 1-second Interval timer
  2. In loop (plutoLoop): When the timer fires, set GPIO_1 HIGH (buzzer ON), then immediately set it LOW (buzzer OFF) — this produces a short beep
  3. On stop (onLoopFinish): Set GPIO_1 LOW to ensure the buzzer is silent

Key APIs

APIPurpose
Peripheral_Init(GPIO_1, OUTPUT)Configure GPIO_1 as an output pin
Peripheral_Write(GPIO_1, STATE_HIGH)Set GPIO_1 HIGH (buzzer ON)
Peripheral_Write(GPIO_1, STATE_LOW)Set GPIO_1 LOW (buzzer OFF)

Solution

#include "PlutoPilot.h"

Interval beepTimer;

void plutoRxConfig(void) {
  Receiver_Mode(Rx_ESP);
}

void plutoInit(void) {
  Peripheral_Init(GPIO_1, OUTPUT);  // Initialize buzzer pin as output
}

void onLoopStart(void) {
  Peripheral_Write(GPIO_1, STATE_LOW);  // Buzzer OFF initially
  beepTimer.set(1000, true);            // Beep every 1 second
}

void plutoLoop(void) {
  if (beepTimer.check()) {
    Peripheral_Write(GPIO_1, STATE_HIGH);  // Buzzer ON (beep)
    Peripheral_Write(GPIO_1, STATE_LOW);   // Buzzer OFF
  }
}

void onLoopFinish(void) {
  Peripheral_Write(GPIO_1, STATE_LOW);  // Ensure buzzer is silent
}
Try This!

⇀ Use a sensor value (e.g., altitude or battery voltage) to change the beep timing
⇀ Make it beep Morse code for a word — great introduction to signal encoding!
⇀ Try connecting an external LED to another GPIO pin for a combined audio-visual alert

ide-dashboard.title: Dashboard & Sign In
ide-dashboard.html:
Beginner

Open the Dashboard

The Dashboard is your home screen inside Pluto IDE. From here you create projects, pick boards and sign in. There are two easy ways to open it:

1

Click the Pluto IDE icon

Look at the row of icons on the far left of VS Code (the Activity Bar) and click the Pluto IDE icon.

2

Or use the Command Palette

Press Ctrl+Shift+P (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS), type Open Dashboard, and press Enter.

Pluto IDE Dashboard — Home tab with New Project button

What’s on the Dashboard

The menu on the left of the dashboard switches between a few simple areas:

AreaWhat it’s for
HomeThe welcome screen, with big New Project and Open Project buttons, latest news, and recent projects.
ProjectA full list of your projects (the last 20 are tracked), plus Create and Open Directory buttons.
BoardsPhotos of every supported flight controller. Click one to see its pin diagrams (Top, Bottom and UniBUS views).
Sign In (top-right)Sign in to your Drona Aviation account.
Follow UsLinks to the Pluto community (Discord, Instagram, GitHub and more).
No internet?

If you’re offline, the news area simply shows “Unable to load news.” — nothing is broken, and the rest of the dashboard works fine.

Sign In (Passwordless)

Pluto IDE uses a “magic link” to sign in — there’s no password to create or remember. You just confirm your email.

1

Click “Sign In”

It’s at the top-right corner of the dashboard.

2

Type your email and send the link

Enter your email address, then click Send magic link.

📷
Screenshot — Sign-in window
assets/images/screenshots/signin-wizard.png
Type your email and click “Send magic link”.
3

Check your email and open the link

You’ll receive an email with a secure sign-in link. Click it — it automatically brings you back into VS Code and signs you in. (No email after a minute? Check your spam folder.)

📷
Screenshot — The magic-link email
assets/images/screenshots/signin-email.png
Open the secure link from your inbox to finish signing in.
4

Fill in your profile (first time only)

If this is a brand-new account, you’ll be asked for a few details — all required:

  • Full Name
  • Email (already filled in)
  • Phone Number
  • Institute / Organization
  • Date of Birth

Returning users skip this and are signed in instantly.

📷
Screenshot — First-time profile form
assets/images/screenshots/profile-form.png
New accounts fill in a short profile once.
Opened the link on your phone?

No problem. Pluto IDE notices and signs you in on your computer automatically — you don’t have to start over.

Why Sign In?

You can try Pluto IDE without an account, but each action (Build, Clean, USB Flash, WiFi Flash, Monitor) can only be used a few times for free. When you have 2 uses left you’ll see a gentle reminder, and after 5 uses you’ll be asked to sign in:

Message you’ll see

“Command limit reached (5 uses). Please sign in to continue using…” — with a Sign In button right there.

Signing in is free and removes the limit completely, so you can build and flash as much as you like. You can also see your usage (build / flash / monitor counts) and, for library projects, keep your code backed up.

Signing Out

After you sign in, the Sign In button is replaced by your user menu in the top-right. Open it and choose Log out whenever you want to sign out.

📷
Screenshot — User menu after signing in
assets/images/screenshots/user-menu.png
Open the user menu in the top-right and choose Log out to sign out.

ide-new-project.title: Create & Open Projects
ide-new-project.html:
Beginner

What is a “Project”?

A project is just a folder on your computer that holds your drone code and everything needed to build it. Pluto IDE creates this folder for you and fills it with a working starting point, so you can jump straight to writing code.

Create a New Project

1

Open the wizard

On the dashboard, click New Project (Home tab) or Create (Project tab).

Fill in the details, choose your board, pick a folder, and click Create Project.
2

Fill in the form

Here’s what each field means:

FieldWhat to enter
Project NameA short name — up to 8 characters, using only letters, numbers, - or _ (no spaces).
DescriptionOptional (up to 200 characters). A short note so you remember what this project does.
BoardChoose your flight controller (see the next card). A photo previews as you pick.
LocationClick Browse and choose the folder where the project will be created.
Include SourcesLeave it as you prefer — explained two cards down.
3

Click “Create Project”

Pluto IDE downloads the firmware template, sets up the project, opens the new folder in VS Code, and adds it to your recent projects.

Tip — good project names

Keep it short, no spaces. Good examples: my-drone, test1, fw-v2.

Choosing Your Board

Pick the option that matches your Pluto. This decides which firmware Pluto IDE downloads for you.

Not sure which board you have?

Open the Boards tab on the dashboard and compare your flight controller with the photos and pin diagrams there.

“Include Sources” — Which Should I Pick?

This one checkbox chooses between two kinds of project:

If you…Then…You get
Just want to write drone logic using the ready-made Pluto commandsLeave it uncheckedLibrary project — only your application code (main.c) is included; the firmware core is linked in as pre-compiled libraries. Quicker and simpler.
Want to change the flight-controller firmware itselfCheck itSource project — the full firmware source code is copied in and the Makefile is fully editable, for complete control over the build.
New here? Start simple

If you’re just getting started, a Library project (unchecked) is the easiest way to begin.

What Happens When You Click Create

You don’t need to do anything during this — here’s what Pluto IDE is doing for you:

  1. Creates your project folder at the location you chose.
  2. Downloads the right firmware for your board (and remembers it, so next time is faster).
  3. Sets your chosen board as the build target.
  4. Sets up code suggestions and error-checking for you.
  5. Opens the project and the main code file ready to edit.
This is where you write your code

Open the main code file (PlutoPilot.cpp for source projects, or main.c for library projects) and write your drone logic there.

Signed in + Library project = automatic backup

If you’re signed in and using a Library project, Pluto IDE can keep your code backed up to the cloud automatically (look for the Auto Sync button in the status bar). If it ever finds a different version saved online, it asks you which one to keep — your local copy or the cloud copy.

Open a Project You Made Before

1

Click Open Project

Use Open Project on the Home tab, Open Directory on the Project tab, or just click a project in your Recent Projects list.

2

Pick the project folder

Choose the folder you created earlier. Pluto IDE remembers your board and reopens your main code file for you.

ide-build.title: Board Select, Build & Flash
ide-build.html:
Beginner

The Buttons You’ll Use

Once a project is open, Pluto IDE adds buttons to the status bar — the strip along the bottom of the VS Code window. Every button also has a matching command in the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P).

📷
Screenshot — Pluto IDE status bar buttons
assets/images/screenshots/status-bar.png
Select Target, Build, Clean, USB Flash, WiFi Flash and Monitor live at the bottom of VS Code.
ButtonCommandWhat it does
Select TargetPlutoIDE > Select TargetChoose which board to build/flash for
BuildPlutoIDE > BuildTurn your code into firmware
CleanPlutoIDE > CleanDelete old build files for a fresh start
USB FlashPlutoIDE > USB FlashUpload firmware using a USB cable
WiFi FlashPlutoIDE > WiFi FlashUpload firmware wirelessly
MonitorPlutoIDE > MonitorSee live data coming from the drone
Install BootloaderPlutoIDE > STM32 Install BootloaderInstall the USB flashing driver (one time)

Step 1 · Select Your Board (Target)

Before building, make sure the right board is selected. Pluto IDE supports these targets:

BoardFirmware familyNotes
PRIMUS_V5Magis V2Latest board
PRIMUS_X2_v1Magis V2Latest board
PRIMUSV4Magis (legacy)Older board
PRIMUSXMagis (legacy)Older board
ALL—Build for all boards in the family at once

Pick your board in either way:

A

Status Bar

Click the Select Target button at the bottom and choose your board.

B

Command Palette

Press Ctrl+Shift+P, run PlutoIDE > Select Target, and choose your board.

📷
Screenshot — Select Target menu
assets/images/screenshots/select-target.png
Pick your board from the list. It’s remembered and shown in the status bar.
Tip

If you don’t pick a target, Pluto IDE will ask you to choose one the moment you try to build.

Step 2 · Build Your Code

Building compiles your code into a firmware file (a .hex / .bin) you can flash.

1

Make sure a target is selected

See Step 1 above.

2

Start the build

Click Build in the status bar, or run PlutoIDE > Build from the Command Palette.

3

Watch the progress

A panel opens at the bottom and shows progress in real time ([0%] → [50%] → [100%]). When you see Build Complete, your firmware is ready to flash.

📷
Screenshot — A successful build
assets/images/screenshots/build-success.png
Build progress reaches 100% and shows “Build Complete”.
Build failed?

Error messages appear in the build panel and point to the problem. Common causes: no target selected, code mistakes, or (on Windows) a project path with spaces — see Troubleshooting.

Step 3 · Clean (Optional)

Click Clean (or run PlutoIDE > Clean) to delete the temporary build files. Your code is never touched — only the generated build output is removed.

When is this useful? Before a fresh full rebuild, to free disk space, or before sharing only your source files. You usually won’t need it day-to-day.

Step 4a · Flash Over USB

Flashing over a cable is the most reliable way to upload. Do a successful Build first.

1

Install the USB driver (first time only)

Run STM32 Install Bootloader once. On Windows, approve the administrator prompt. This is mainly needed on Windows and only the first time.

2

Connect the drone with USB

Plug your Pluto into the computer. Pluto IDE detects it in flashing (DFU) mode automatically.

3

Click USB Flash

Click USB Flash (or run PlutoIDE > USB Flash). The firmware is found and uploaded automatically, with progress shown as it goes.

4

Power-cycle the drone

When it finishes, turn the drone off and on again so it starts running your new firmware.

📷
Screenshot — USB flashing in progress
assets/images/screenshots/usb-flash.png
USB Flash uploads your firmware over the cable, then asks you to power-cycle the drone.
“Device not detected”?

Install the STM32 bootloader driver, make sure the drone is connected, and try a different USB cable or port.

Step 4b · Flash Over WiFi

No cable? Upload wirelessly over the drone’s own WiFi — no driver needed. Build first.

1

Turn on the drone

Power up your Pluto. After a few seconds it broadcasts its own WiFi network (a “hotspot”).

2

Connect your computer to the drone’s WiFi

Open your computer’s WiFi settings and join the drone’s network — its name contains Pluto, Drone or Demo.

3

Make sure nothing else is connected

Close the Pluto Controller app and disconnect the camera module if you were using them — only one thing can talk to the drone at a time.

4

Click WiFi Flash

Click WiFi Flash (or run PlutoIDE > WiFi Flash). The firmware uploads wirelessly — wait for the Done message.

📷
Screenshot — WiFi flashing
assets/images/screenshots/wifi-flash.png
After joining the drone’s WiFi, WiFi Flash uploads wirelessly.
“Wrong Wi-Fi selected”?

Your computer isn’t on the drone’s WiFi. Switch to the drone’s hotspot (Pluto / Drone / Demo) and click WiFi Flash again.

USB vs WiFi — Which Should I Use?

USB FlashWiFi Flash
NeedsA USB cable + the one-time driver (Windows)Nothing but WiFi — no driver
Speed & reliabilityFastest and most reliableConvenient, no cable
Best forFirst-time setup, or if WiFi flashing failsQuick updates while testing

Step 5 · Watch Live Data with Monitor

The Monitor button opens a terminal showing live messages from your drone — sensor data, motor status and debug output — handy for checking your code works.

1

Connect to the drone’s WiFi

Monitor works over WiFi, so power on the drone and join its WiFi network (just like WiFi flashing).

2

Click Monitor

Live data starts streaming in. Run Monitor again to toggle it off. For graphs over time, use the bundled Teleplot view.

📷
Screenshot — Pluto Monitor
assets/images/screenshots/monitor.png
Monitor streams live data from the drone over WiFi.

Bonus · See the Pin Diagrams

Need to know which pin is which? On the dashboard, open the Boards tab and click your board. A viewer opens with Top, Bottom and UniBUS views you can swipe through.

📷
Screenshot — Board pinout viewer
assets/images/screenshots/boards-pinout.png
Click a board on the Boards tab to flip through its Top, Bottom and UniBUS pin diagrams.

ide-troubleshooting.title: Troubleshooting
ide-troubleshooting.html:
Beginner

Setup & Activation

ProblemFix
Toolchain setup failsCheck your internet connection. Delete the tools folder (C:\PlutoIDE\tools\ on Windows, ~/.pluto-ide/tools/ on macOS/Linux) and restart VS Code — the tools re-download automatically.
Extension does not activateMake sure the C/C++ extension is installed, then restart VS Code. If it persists, uninstall and reinstall Pluto IDE.
Dashboard does not openCheck your VS Code version is up to date, then reload the window: Ctrl+Shift+P › Developer: Reload Window.
“make” command not found (Windows)The Cygwin install may be incomplete. Verify make.exe exists in C:\PlutoIDE\tools\cygwin64\bin\. If missing, delete the tools folder and restart VS Code.

Building

ProblemFix
Build failsMake sure a target board is selected (Select Target). On Windows, if your project path contains spaces, move it to a simple path like C:\Projects\.
Firmware file not generated / not visibleEven after a successful build, if the file isn’t showing, reload the window: Ctrl+Shift+P › Developer: Reload Window.
“No target selected”Click Select Target in the status bar, choose your board, then build again.
“plutoide.ini not found”The folder you opened isn’t a Pluto project. Open the folder you created with the New Project wizard.

Flashing & Connection

ProblemFix
USB flash: device not detectedInstall the STM32 Bootloader driver, make sure the drone is connected, and try a different USB cable or port.
WiFi flash not working / “Wrong Wi-Fi selected”Confirm your computer is joined to the drone’s WiFi (name contains Pluto / Drone / Demo), check the WiFi password, and restart the drone if needed.
“HEX file not found”There’s nothing to flash yet — run Build successfully first.
“Command limit reached (5 uses)”You’ve used your free actions. Click Sign In — it’s free and removes the limit.

Golden Rules for Flashing

  • Always Build before you Flash. Flashing uploads the firmware that Build creates.
  • Only one connection at a time. When flashing or monitoring over WiFi, close the Pluto Controller app and disconnect the camera.
  • Power-cycle after a USB flash so the drone runs your new firmware.
  • USB not working? Try WiFi (and vice-versa).
